Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette:
# Thien's Vigil

Thien Nguyen was fifty-eight when his eldest son drowned during the monsoon season off the coast of Galveston. The boy—Duc, who was twenty-three—had gone out on a commercial fishing boat with two of Thien's regular crew members, men Thien had known for nearly thirty years. The boat capsized in a sudden squall. The other two men were pulled from the water by the coast guard. Duc was found four hours later, face-down in the churn, already cold.

Thien had been on the dock that morning, mending nets as he had done for forty years. He watched Duc walk toward the boat, saw his son wave back at him with that careless confidence of the young. The last thing Duc said was, "Don't worry, Papa. We'll be back before dark." They never came back. When the coast guard called, Thien's hands had still been tangled in the net. He had to cut himself free.

In the days after the funeral, Thien's wife, Linh, noticed he barely slept. He would lie beside her in the dark, staring at nothing, his body rigid. When he did drift off, he would jerk awake, gasping, his heart hammering so hard she could feel it through the mattress. Sometimes he would call out Duc's name. Within a week, Thien had stopped trying to sleep in the bedroom at all. He moved to the living room couch, where he would sit upright until dawn, waiting for something he could not name.

The physical reactions came without warning. A car door slamming in the driveway sent a spike of adrenaline through his chest so violent he thought he was having a heart attack. The sound of water—even from the shower, even from the kitchen faucet—made his palms sweat and his breathing shallow. Once, Linh turned on the television and a news report about a fishing accident in Louisiana came on. Thien's whole body went rigid. His face drained of color. He stood up, walked to the bedroom, and closed the door. He didn't come out for two hours.

What had begun to crystallize in Thien's mind, in the weeks that followed, was a conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that the people in it could not be trusted. The two crew members who survived—men he had called friends—had come to the house to pay respects. Thien had listened to their account of what happened, and something in their words felt false to him. Why had they been pulled from the water so quickly? Why had Duc not been found until later? He had come to believe, though he could not articulate it clearly, that there was something they were not telling him. Perhaps they had not tried hard enough. Perhaps they had chosen themselves. He stopped answering their calls.

His wife had begun to feel like a stranger too. She would try to comfort him, to sit with him on the couch at night, and he would feel nothing—no warmth from her presence, no solace in her touch. She seemed to exist on the other side of a thick glass wall. He loved her, he knew this intellectually, but the feeling itself had drained away, leaving only a hollow space where his capacity for connection used to be. "I feel dead inside," he told her once, and she had wept. He had not been able to comfort her.

The guilt had become a constant companion. Why had he sent Duc out that day? Why had he not warned him about the weather, which he—a man who had read the ocean his entire life—had sensed was turning dangerous? Other fishermen's sons had survived. Other families still had their boys. The unfairness of it, the randomness, made no sense to him. He had come to believe that his survival, his continued breathing and walking and eating, was somehow unjust. He did not deserve to be here when Duc was not.

By his sixtieth birthday, Thien had stopped going to the docks entirely. His wife had tried to coax him back, saying the business needed him, that the crew was struggling without him. But the thought of being near the water, of hearing the boats, of seeing the nets—all of it felt like a punishment he could not bear. He had effectively retired, though no one had said it aloud. The income had dried up. Linh had taken a job at a grocery store to keep them afloat. She came home exhausted, and Thien sat in the living room, waiting for sleep that would not come, waiting for the guilt to somehow transform into something he could survive.

It was Linh who finally insisted he see someone. She had found a therapist who specialized in grief and trauma. Thien had resisted, but his wife's quiet desperation had worn through his resistance. He had agreed to one appointment, telling himself it would change nothing. What he did not yet understand was that the wall between him and the rest of the world had become so thick that he could no longer see through it—and that somewhere, beneath the numbness and the guilt and the fear, a part of him still wanted to.
